newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-French share rally seen running out of steam.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French share rally seen running out of steam.

text.p: The French share rally that has taken prices to historic highs is running out of steam and the market is likely to succumb to profit-taking soon and then stay flat until the second half of 1997, analysts said on Wednesday.
Wall Street's recent record performance has pulled French shares out of the doldrums, but some investors are getting vertigo and fund managers are reviewing their options.
The CAC-40 index of blue-chip shares, fell 17.75 points, or 0.71 percent, to close at 2,465.01 on Wednesday on the back of a dollar downturn. It hit a historic high of 2,484.26 on Tuesday.
That represents a climb from 2,256.97 at the start of the year and all the way from a low of 1,974.67 in July 1996.

"I remain bullish on this market and I see it going to 2,650/2,700 at the year-end. But I expected it to rise to 2,500 at the middle of the year and we're nearly there. There has to be some profit-taking soon after which the market is likely to be flat for some time," an analyst at brokerage IFF said.
Bryan Allworth at Merrill Lynch expects the CAC-40 to be at 2,400 in three months' time, rising to 2,700 at the end of the year, implying a correction in the coming weeks.
"I don't see a real improvement until the end of the second quarter or in the second half. There have to be some really good corporate earnings to justify the current levels," he said.
Markus Roesgen at Morgan Stanley saw the index declining to 2,050 by the end of the year and Caroline Meroz at J.P. Morgan maintained her target at 2,450.
"We are underweight on France. We are confident of growth potential in 1998, but not for 1997," Meroz said.
As always, the French stock market is very much influenced by developments on Wall Street as well as the dollar and interest rate developments.
The French market clearly underperformed Wall Street, London and other major markets in 1995 and 1996.

While the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the FTSE-100 index posted repeated records during the past two years, the French blue-chip index was depressed by such domestic factors as the presidential elections, social unrest and doubts -- now less widespread -- about France's ability to meet the Maastricht Treaty criteria for a single European currency.
An upturn in economic growth and the steady decline in interest rates fanned hopes of a recovery in corporate earnings.
These hopes, coupled with Wall Street's rise and an abundance of start-of-year funds, boosted the Paris market in January to a series of record highs.
The first 1996 corporate results, with big advances at Rhone-Poulenc Rorer, Totaland Elf Aquitaine, confirmed the market's optimism but also raised questions about the sustainability of profits.
CAC-40 shares are currently trading on average at 19 times expected 1996 earnings per share and at 20.5 times the expected 1997 results.
The average dividend yield, based on 1995 results, is a low 1.9 percent.
"The problem with these high share prices is that we need to see big increases in dividend to generate an unchanged yield," an analyst said.
Interest rates, with the intervention rate of 3.15 percent at an historic low, are expected by some economists to come down to 3.00 percent, but no further.
